sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Pángǔ** (*pangu*) — The Giant Between Heaven and Earth — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Creation, Separation, Foundation". The name means "'Coiled antiquity' (盤古), the giant who split heaven from earth"[^1].

Pángǔ is China's creation made flesh: the giant who grew for eighteen thousand years inside the cosmic egg, pushed heaven and earth apart with his own body, and — dying at last — became the world itself: his eyes the sun and moon, his breath the wind, his voice the thunder.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Pángǔ** and serves its temple at [pángǔ.com](https://xn--png-ela13j.com). The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *pangu* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.
Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.
Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Pángǔ** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "'Coiled antiquity' (盤古), the giant who split heaven from earth"[^1].

The ASCII form *pangu* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Pángǔ** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original preserves one prosodic feature — stress or vowel length — rather than both, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **p** → **P** — Same letter
- **a** → **á** — Stress mark (acute/tone)
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **g** → **g** — Same letter
- **u** → **ǔ** — same

The project holds the domain **pángǔ.com** (xn--png-ela13j.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Chen Shou, Sanguozhi (Records of the Three Kingdoms), Zhonghua Shuju critical edition, 289.
Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/pʰa˧˥ ku˨˩˦/** — Mandarin (Hanyu Pinyin with tones).[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: pahng-goo, rising tone on Pang, low-dipping on Gu.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — 盤古
- **Owned form** — Pángǔ

Pángǔ 盘古 carries the rising tone on páng and the dipping third tone on gǔ ("antiquity"); the name pairs "coiling" with "ancient" — the coiled one of the primordial egg. Written 盤古 in traditional characters, it is Chinese myth's youngest great name: the giant is attested only from the 3rd century CE.

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The original script for this chinese name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Pángǔ** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

Written 盘古 (盤古 traditional): pán (coil, tray, the great basin) plus gǔ (ancient). The graphs describe him exactly — the coiled giant of antiquity, curled inside the cosmic egg before there was a world to be ancient in.

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Pángǔ is China's creation made flesh: the giant who grew for eighteen thousand years inside the cosmic egg, pushed heaven and earth apart with his own body, and — dying at last — became the world itself: his eyes the sun and moon, his breath the wind, his voice the thunder.[^1]

### The Cosmic Egg

Chaos like a hen's egg — and Pángǔ born within it, the first form in the formless.

### The Separation

Heaven rose ten feet daily, earth thickened ten feet, and he grew between them — 18,000 years of pushing.

### The Transformation

His body becomes the world: eyes to sun and moon, limbs to mountains, blood to rivers.

### The Chisel and Axe

Folk art arms him with the tools of separation — the first worker, carving sky from stone.

sources.citation: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Pángǔ concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The egg** — Chaos as potential — the undivided whole that must crack to become a world
- **The horns** — His folk-iconography — the shaggy, horned giant of the first morning
- **The pillars of his limbs** — The four limbs as the four sacred mountains — the body as geography

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Pángǔ's myth exists in two sentences of immense consequence, recorded by Xú Zhěng in the 3rd century CE — and expanded by a civilization into its canonical account of how the world began.[^1]

### Three-Five Calendar Record (The Egg)

Xú Zhěng's Sānwǔ lìjì gives the founding text: "Heaven and earth were chaos like a hen's egg, and Pángǔ was born within it. After eighteen thousand years, heaven and earth opened: the bright, light qì rose to become heaven; the dark, heavy qì sank to become earth. Pángǔ stood between them, changing nine times daily — heaven rising ten feet a day, earth thickening ten feet, and Pángǔ growing ten feet — for eighteen thousand years more."[^2]

### The Body Becomes the World (The Death)

When the separation was fixed, Pángǔ died — and the transformation began: his breath became wind and cloud, his voice thunder, his left eye the sun and his right the moon, his four limbs the four sacred mountains, his blood the rivers, his veins the roads, his flesh the soil, his hair the stars, his skin and body-hair grass and trees, his sweat rain — and, in the most anthropologically piquant line, his fleas and lice, quickened by the wind, became the black-haired people.

### China's Youngest Creator (The Late Arrival)

The myth's strangest fact is its date: no pre-Han text mentions Pángǔ, and scholars trace his entry through southern traditions — the Yao and Miao genealogies of the dog-ancestor Pán Hù, phonetically adjacent — absorbed and cosmicized in the Wei-Jin centuries. China's canonical creation is thus a relative newcomer, adopted so completely that every schoolchild now learns it as the oldest story.

sources.citation: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1993.
Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), Sima Qian; Chinese Text Project, 91 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Pángǔ–Pán Hù debate is one of Chinese mythology's famous problems: the southern dog-ancestor of the Yao and She peoples and the cosmic giant share a syllable and a region, and scholars from the Republican era onward have argued transmission in both directions. Comparative mythology places him with the dismembered primordial beings — Vedic Púruṣa, Norse Ymir — whose bodies become worlds: China's version is distinctive for making the giant's death not a murder but a completion.[^1]

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], [[long|Lóng]], [[mengpo|Méngpó]], and [[nuwa|Nǚwā]].

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: "Since Pángǔ separated heaven and earth" is the standard Chinese formula for "since the beginning of time," and his myth opens every children's account of Chinese prehistory. The transformation — body to landscape — gave Chinese poetry one of its deepest image-families, the mountain-as-body. UNESCO-listed school textbooks, animated films, and the giant's statues across southern China (Henan's Tongbai county claims his birthplace) keep the youngest creator as the most familiar.[^1]

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No cult-temple of Pángǔ predates the myth's literary arrival, but his material afterlife is real: the Pángǔ temples of Tongbai (Henan) and the southern shrines of Guangdong and Guangxi mark the festival of his "birth" in the tenth lunar month. The textual archaeology is exact — Xú Zhěng's Sānwǔ lìjì and the Wǔyùn lìnián jì (both 3rd century, preserved in encyclopedias) are the two struts of the whole tradition, and the history of their quotation is the history of the myth itself.[^1]

His cult is young, like his myth: the **Pángǔ temple of Tongbai county** (Henan) anchors the tradition's claimed birthplace, with his festival in the tenth lunar month drawing the county's pilgrimage. In the south — Guangdong and Guangxi, where scholars trace the myth's Yao and Miao ancestry — village shrines to Pángǔ dàrén, 'the great man Pangu,' predate the literary fame. The **Museum of Chinese creation mythology** tradition apart, his monuments are the mountains themselves: the myth names them his limbs, and the pilgrim reads the landscape as the giant's body, which is the oldest way of reading it.

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.
Birrell, Chinese Mythology; the Tongbai temple records.

sections.label: Classical Texts
sections.body:
The youngest creator has the simplest titles.

- **Pángǔ shì** — 'Master Pangu'; the respectful vernacular address.
- **Kāitiān pìdì** — 'who separated heaven and earth'; the title that is also the idiom for absolute beginnings.
- **Shǐzǔ** — 'the First Ancestor'; the genealogical title of the southern temples.
- **Hùndùn zhī zǐ** — 'child of Chaos'; the mythic lineage-name.
- **Yǔzhòu zhī shēn** — 'the Body of the Universe'; the doctrinal title of the transformation myth.

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji; Birrell, Chinese Mythology (Pangu).

sections.label: Daoist Sources
sections.body: Daoist cosmology adopted him wholesale: the *Yunji Qiqian* and the Daoist creation treatises retell the egg and the eighteen thousand years within the vocabulary of qì — the light and heavy vapors he separates are the tradition's own. Some registers deify him further as a primordial lord of the first era, and the flood-and-egg cosmogonies of the southern textual traditions (where scholars trace his Yao and Miao ancestry) circulate in Daoist-liturgical editions. China's youngest creator became, in the canon, simply the name for the beginning.

sources.citation: Yunji Qiqian (creation treatises); Birrell, Chinese Mythology.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Buddhist Sources
sections.body: Buddhist cosmologies, rich in their own world-cycles, took him up late and locally: vernacular Buddhist storytelling syncretizes the egg with the kalpa's re-formation after the cosmic winds destroy the old world, and temple-wall narratives in the south place him before the Buddha's eras as the previous formation's giant. The scholarly engagement is equally real: the Buddhist encyclopedias' discussions of non-Buddhist origins cite the Pángǔ myth as China's native answer to the kalpa.

sources.citation: The Buddhist cosmological encyclopedias; Birrell, Chinese Mythology.

sections.label: Calligraphy & Script
sections.body: 盘古 (盤古): pán (盤) is the great basin — dish with the boat-phonetic — evoking the coiled container of chaos; gǔ (古) is "ancient," ten mouths, the tradition handed down. Together: the coiled one of antiquity. The name is young as names go — third century CE — and its graphs are transparent where older gods' are opaque, a name written to describe. Temple steles of the Tongbai and southern shrines carve the pair in the standard script of their centuries: a creation story told, fittingly, in plain characters.

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji; the Tongbai temple steles.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Pángǔ is the god of the long work: eighteen thousand years of pushing, unnoticed, until the sky stayed up on its own. He never saw the world he made — he became it. He asks of everyone engaged in slow, unglamorous creation: what are you growing between the heaven and the earth of your time — and will it stand when you are done?

The flea-born people of the oldest version keep the myth honest: humanity is not the giant's masterpiece but his smallest parasite, quickened by the wind. It is the humblest creation-line in world mythology — and somehow the most accurate: we are the detail, not the design, and the world was not made for us but of something that once stood up and held it apart.[^1]

sources.citation: Xu Zheng, Sanwu Liji (Historical Records of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors), as preserved in later encyclopedias (Taiping Yulan), 260.
